title: Nodes and edges in code
objectives: Store a graph as an adjacency list and as a matrix.
Choose between them by space and by the question asked

screens.title: Who is joined to whom
screens.prose: Six nodes, A to F. Each line is an **edge** joining two of them. In code we need a way to store exactly this picture.
screens.question: Tap every node joined to C by an edge.

hints.text: Follow each line that leaves C.
Three lines leave C.
The lines from C end at A, D and E.

feedback.correct: C is joined to A, D and E.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the nodes at the other end of a line from C.

byKey.B: B is two edges from C, through A or D. Tap only nodes one line away.
byKey.F: F is joined to E, not to C. Tap only nodes one line away from C.
byKey.C: C itself is not joined to C here. Tap the nodes at the other ends of its lines.

explain.text: A, D and E are C's **neighbours**. If a program knows each node's neighbours, it knows the whole graph. That is the first way to store one.

screens.title: A list per node
screens.prose: Write down every node's neighbours, in alphabetical order. Row A is done for you.
screens.question: Fill in the neighbours of B to F, separated by commas.

hints.text: For each node, follow every line that touches it.
F has one line only.
B: A, D. C: A, D, E. D: B, C. E: C, F. F: E.

feedback.correct: Each node has its own list of neighbours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the amber rows against the lines in the drawing.

byKey.r2c1: Check C again: it has three lines, to A, D and E.
byKey.r3c1: D touches B and C. An edge counts at both of its ends.
byKey.r5c1: F has a single line, to E.

explain.text: You wrote an **adjacency list**. In Python it is a dict of lists: `{"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["A", "D"], ...}`. Edge A–B appears twice, once in A's list and once in B's.

screens.title: A grid of 0s and 1s
screens.prose: The same graph as a grid. Row $i$, column $j$ holds 1 when nodes $i$ and $j$ share an edge, else 0. Row C is blank.
screens.question: Fill in row C.

hints.text: C's neighbours are A, D and E. Which columns are those?
Row A already shows the pattern: 1 under B and under C.
Put 1 under A, D and E, and 0 under B, C and F.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put 1 in each column that is a neighbour of C, and 0 elsewhere.

byKey.r0c2: C has no edge to itself here, so the diagonal cell is 0.
byKey.r0c1: B is not joined to C, so that cell is 0.
byKey.r0c5: F is joined to E, not to C, so that cell is 0.

explain.text: This grid is the **adjacency matrix**, a list of lists. `M[2][3]` answers "is C joined to D?" in one step. Row C matches column C, because every edge works both ways.

screens.prose: Here is the whole matrix. The graph has 6 edges.
screens.question: How many 1s does the matrix hold?

widget.label: Number of 1s
widget.accept: 12: each of the 6 edges is stored twice.

hints.text: Count the 1s row by row.
Row C holds three 1s.
The rows hold 2, 2, 3, 2, 2 and 1: that is 12.

feedback.correct: 12 ones for 6 edges: each edge appears twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the 1s in each row and add them up.

byKey.edges: You counted each edge once. Edge A–B sets row A, column B and also row B, column A.
byKey.cells: 36 is every cell, the 0s included. Count only the 1s.

explain.text: Edge C–D puts a 1 at row C, column D and at row D, column C. So an undirected graph's matrix is symmetric, with $2E$ ones. It still has $V^2 = 36$ cells, whatever the number of edges.

screens.title: One-way edges with weights
screens.prose: A currency graph is **directed**. An arrow from GBP to USD means you can sell pounds for dollars at that rate. Each edge also carries a **weight**, the rate.
screens.question: Which dict stores this graph?

options.why: You stored each arrow at both ends. A directed edge lives only in the list of the node it leaves.
You left JPY out because no arrow leaves it. It is still a node, and `adj["JPY"]` would raise `KeyError`.
You kept who links to whom but dropped the rates. A weighted graph stores (neighbour, weight) pairs.

hints.text: For each currency, list only the arrows that leave it.
No arrow leaves JPY. Does it still need a key?
Each arrow is one (neighbour, rate) pair in its start node's list, and JPY gets an empty list.

feedback.correct: One (neighbour, rate) pair per arrow, stored at the arrow's start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Store each arrow once, at the node it leaves, with its rate.

explain.text: A directed edge goes in one list only, so a directed graph's matrix need not be symmetric. A node with no outgoing edges still gets a key with an empty list. Level 2 searches a graph like this for a loop of trades that makes money.

screens.title: Build the list from edges
screens.prose: Data usually arrives as an **edge list**: one pair per edge. Return a dict mapping every node to a sorted list of its neighbours. A self-loop `(u, u)` puts `u` in its own list once.
screens.question: Write `adj_list(nodes, edges)` for an undirected graph.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, including a node with no edges, a self-loop and an empty graph. Each dict must equal the expected one exactly.

hints.text: Start with an empty list for every node, then walk the edges.
Edge A–B must land in A's list and in B's.
`adj = {v: [] for v in nodes}`. For each `(u, v)`: append `v` to `adj[u]`, and `u` to `adj[v]` unless `u == v`. Sort each list.

feedback.correct: Every node has a key, every edge is stored at both ends, and a self-loop once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects each edge at both ends. Append `u` to `adj[v]` as well as `v` to `adj[u]`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has a node C with no edges. Build the dict from `nodes`, not from the edges, so C maps to `[]`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has the self-loop `("X", "X")`. Adding both ends puts X in its own list twice; add it once.

explain.text: Building from `nodes` first keeps isolated nodes. Each edge costs two appends, so the build takes $O(V + E)$ time and the dict holds $2E$ entries. Sorting is only there to make the output fixed.

screens.title: The missing half
screens.prose:
A colleague builds the list like this, with the same six edges.

```python
adj = {v: [] for v in "ABCDEF"}
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
print(adj["D"])
```

state.caption: D has two edges in the drawing

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read D's edges off the drawing. The loop only appends to `adj[u]`, and D is always the second name of its pairs.
The dict comprehension gives every letter a key first, so `adj["D"]` exists. It is just empty.
You stored the edge from C, but `("C", "D")` appends D to C's list, not C to D's.

hints.text: In which pairs does D appear, and in which position?
D's edges are B–D and C–D.
Both pairs have D second. The loop appends D to B's and C's lists, and nothing to D's.

feedback.correct: D's list is empty: the reverse edges were never stored.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the loop by hand for the pairs that contain D.

byKey.both: You expected each edge to be stored both ways. This loop stores `(u, v)` only in `adj[u]`, so D, always second, gets nothing.
byKey.one: You stored C–D at D's end. The loop appends only to the first name's list.

explain.text: The loop treats each pair as a one-way arrow. A search started at D would find no neighbours and stop at once, with no error. For an undirected graph add `adj[v].append(u)` on the next line.

canvas.caption: Stored only as B → D and C → D

screens.title: List or matrix
screens.prose:
With $V$ nodes and $E$ edges:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{list: } & O(V + E) \text{ space, neighbours of } u \text{ in } O(\deg u) \\ \text{matrix: } & O(V^2) \text{ space, is } u \text{ joined to } v \text{ in } O(1) \end{aligned}$$

Most real graphs are **sparse**: $E$ is far below $V^2$.
screens.question: A graph of 100,000 firms, each trading with about 20 others. How many cells would its matrix have?

options.why: That is the number of list entries, 100,000 × 20. The matrix has a cell for every pair, traded or not.
That is the number of edges: 100,000 × 20 / 2. The matrix size does not depend on the edges.
That is one cell per firm. A matrix has a row and a column for every firm.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A matrix has one cell for every pair of firms, $V^2$ in all.

explain.text: $10^{10}$ cells as Python lists of 8-byte pointers is about 80 GB, almost all zeros. The adjacency list holds 2 million entries, tens of megabytes. Use a matrix only for small or dense graphs, or when edge checks dominate.

screens.title: Build the matrix
screens.prose: Now the matrix, with nodes numbered 0 to $n - 1$. Watch the first line: `[[0] * n] * n` makes $n$ references to **one** row list.
screens.question: Write `adj_matrix(n, edges)` for an undirected graph: a list of $n$ lists of $n$ zeros, with 1 for each edge.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Nodes are numbered 0 to n − 1. Each matrix must equal the expected list of lists exactly.

hints.text: Make a fresh row for each node, then set two cells per edge.
Rows A and D differ, so they must be different lists.
`m = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]`, then for each `(u, v)` set `m[u][v] = 1` and `m[v][u] = 1`.

feedback.correct: Each row is its own list, and each edge sets two cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: If every row came out the same, the rows are one shared list. Build them with `[[0] * n for _ in range(n)]`.

explain.text: `[[0] * n] * n` repeats a reference to one row, so setting `m[0][1]` sets column 1 in every row. The comprehension builds $n$ separate rows. Building costs $O(V^2)$ before a single edge is read.

screens.title: Finding the clearing house
screens.prose: Each pair `(a, b)` means firm `a` posts margin to firm `b`. A **central counterparty** receives margin from every other firm and posts to none. There is at most one.
screens.question: Write `find_ccp(n, posts)`: return the central counterparty's number, or −1 if there is none.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Firms are numbered 0 to n − 1, and each pair appears at most once. Return the firm's number, or −1.

hints.text: You need two counts per firm: arrows in and arrows out.
Firm 3 has 3 arrows in and none out.
Count `into[b]` and `out[a]` for each pair. Return the firm with `into == n - 1` and `out == 0`, else −1.

feedback.correct: Two degree counts in one pass find it in $O(V + E)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: In test 3 firm 2 receives from both others but also posts to 0. A counterparty posts to nobody.
byKey.test-4: In test 4 firm 2 posts to nobody, but nobody needs to post to it. Check `into == n - 1`.
byKey.test-5: With one firm there is nobody else to receive from, so firm 0 qualifies: `into == 0 == n - 1`.

explain.text: Arrows into a node are its **in-degree**, arrows out its **out-degree**. One pass over the pairs fills both counts, with no list or matrix needed. The same counts start the task-ordering method in lesson 5.

ideas: An adjacency list maps each node to its neighbours: a dict of lists, $O(V + E)$ space. Every node gets a key, even one with no edges.
An adjacency matrix is a $V \times V$ list of lists: $O(V^2)$ space, but `M[u][v]` answers an edge check in one step.
An undirected edge is stored at both ends, and a directed edge only at its start. A weighted edge is stored as a (neighbour, weight) pair.

formula.name: Space
formula.note: Most real graphs are sparse, so the list wins.

summary.trap: Appending only `adj[u].append(v)` for an undirected graph loses every reverse edge, silently.

quiz.prose: An undirected graph has 7 edges and no self-loops.
quiz.question: How many entries do its neighbour lists hold in total?

widget.label: Total entries
widget.accept: 14: each edge appears in two lists.

feedback.correct: Each edge sits in the lists of both its ends: $2 \times 7 = 14$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many lists one edge appears in.

byKey.once: You counted each edge once. Edge u–v appears in u's list and in v's.
byKey.sq: 49 is $E^2$, which measures nothing here. Each edge adds two entries.

explain.text: Edge u–v adds v to u's list and u to v's list. So the lists hold $2E = 14$ entries.

quiz.prose: A surveillance check asks, many times a second, whether two given firms out of 500 have traded with each other.
quiz.question: Which store answers each check fastest?

options.text: The adjacency list: test `j in adj[i]`
options.why: That scans firm i's list, up to $\deg(i)$ comparisons per check. The matrix reads one cell.

options.text: The edge list: test `(i, j) in edges`
options.why: That scans every edge, $O(E)$ per check, and misses `(j, i)` written the other way round.

feedback.correct: One cell read per check, and 500 × 500 cells is small.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps each check takes.

explain.text: With 500 firms the matrix has 250,000 cells, which fits easily. Each check is then one read, $O(1)$. A dict of sets would also give $O(1)$ checks with less space.

quiz.prose: A graph has 1,000 nodes and 3,000 edges.
quiz.question: How many cells does its adjacency matrix have?

widget.label: Cells
widget.accept: 1,000,000: one cell per pair of nodes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The matrix has a row and a column for every node.

byKey.list: That is the list's size, $V + 2E$. The matrix needs $V^2$ cells.
byKey.edges2: That is the number of 1s, $2E$. The 0s take cells too.

explain.text: A matrix has $V^2 = 10^6$ cells whatever the edges. Only $2E = 6{,}000$ hold a 1, so 99.4% of the matrix stores nothing.

quiz.prose:
A data pipeline's steps, as a directed edge list:

```python
edges = [("load", "clean"), ("clean", "score")]
adj = {v: [] for v in ["load", "clean", "score"]}
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
```
quiz.question: What is `adj["score"]`?

options.why: You stored the arrow at both ends. In a directed graph `("clean", "score")` goes only in clean's list.
Every step gets a key from the comprehension, so score exists with an empty list.

feedback.correct: No arrow leaves score, so its list is empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In a directed graph, each arrow is stored only at its start.

explain.text: Here one-way storage is right: the arrows are directed. score is the last step, so nothing follows it and its list is `[]`.
